lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Gisele Gallego | Lesson 9 -- Back to Work

listenings.text: Hi, before we go any further, let me tell you how this actually works here, because people always ask. There are three steps. First, a twenty-minute call with me, and that one is really just to check that the role and your track record line up. Then the hiring manager, his name is Paul, and that conversation is a full hour, and it is the one that matters. Last, a short chat with two people you would work with every day, and honestly, that one is about whether you would be a good fit. The whole thing takes about three weeks. What do I look at first? Not the school. I look at what you took ownership of, and whether you can explain it in plain words. And the biggest mistake, by far? Candidates who never ask anything. At the end I always say, do you have any questions for me, and half of them say no. Please do not be that person.

Hi Gisele, this is Mark Dyson from Halston Group. I am calling about the systems analyst role in Washington, the hybrid one you applied to on Tuesday. So, good news, the hiring manager wants to talk. I am going to try you again tomorrow morning, around ten your time, and if you miss me, do not worry, I will leave the number again. Two things I need from you by email before that call. One, a one-page version of your resume. One page, I mean it, nobody reads three. And two, just a line or two about your notice period, or, in your case, about when you would actually be able to start, since I understand you have been on a career break. Send those over by Thursday at five, because the team closes the list on Friday and I would hate for you to miss it. Okay, talk tomorrow. Bye.

Can I tell you the thing I wish somebody had told me? Stop apologizing for the gap. I hear it in every second interview, I am sorry, I was out for a year, and the apology does more damage than the year ever did. A career break is a line on a page. What people actually want to know is whether you are still the person who takes ownership of things, and eighteen months at home does not change that. And here is what nobody says out loud. Starting over in a country that is not yours is the hardest project management job there is. New systems, new language, a whole family to move, everything late and nothing where you left it. That is not a hole in your track record. Those are transferable skills, and they are the ones that never show up on anybody's resume. So say it like a fact. I took a career break. Here is what I did with it.
